front: A researcher tests whether a new revision method improves scores but reports a significant effect that is actually due to chance. Name the error.
back:
Model answer

This is a Type I error: the researcher rejects a true null hypothesis and concludes an effect exists when it does not.

Marking points

  • Identify Type I
  • Define in null-hypothesis terms
  • Apply to the scenario

Common trap

Do not confuse a false positive with a Type II error.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Psychology 7182 – Mark Scheme::Assessment skills::Statistics

front: A researcher wants to study revision habits across a sixth form but recruits only friends from one psychology class. Explain one sampling problem and one improvement.
back:
Model answer

This is an opportunity sample from one class, so it may over-represent psychology students or the researcher’s social group and may not reflect the sixth-form population. Use a sampling frame and stratified random sampling across year groups or subjects to improve representativeness.

Marking points

  • Name the sampling method/problem
  • Link selection bias to the target population
  • Describe a feasible improvement

Common trap

Do not treat a convenient sample as representative of the whole sixth form.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Psychology 7182 – Mark Scheme::Assessment skills::Sampling

front: A researcher records each participant’s exact reaction time in milliseconds and wants to show its distribution. Choose a display and justify it.
back:
Model answer

A histogram is suitable because reaction time is continuous numerical data; adjacent bars represent intervals and show the distribution. A frequency table can accompany it if exact grouped frequencies are needed.

Marking points

  • Identify continuous measurement
  • Choose histogram
  • Explain touching bars/interval distribution

Common trap

Do not treat the two experimental conditions as bars in a histogram.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Psychology 7182 – Mark Scheme::Assessment skills::Displays

front: A researcher asks pupils about peer pressure using a face-to-face interview. Propose a question format and one design safeguard.
back:
Model answer

Use open questions such as “Can you describe a time a friend influenced a choice you made?” to obtain detail. Pilot the schedule to identify leading or unclear wording; explain confidentiality and allow participants to skip questions.

Marking points

  • Match question format to desired data
  • Give a specific non-leading question or pilot refinement
  • Address one relevant ethical safeguard

Common trap

Do not use a leading question that assumes peer pressure occurred.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Psychology 7182 – Mark Scheme::Assessment skills::Self-report

front: Explain how consistency and flexibility can both help a minority influence a majority.
back:
Model answer

Consistency makes the minority's position salient and signals confidence; flexibility prevents it appearing dogmatic and allows negotiation. Together they can prompt deeper consideration and gradual social change.

Marking points

  • Explain each mechanism and reconcile
  • stay within minority-influence theory.

Common trap

Claiming flexibility means abandoning the core position.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Psychology 7182 – Mark Scheme::Social influence

front: A study ranks participants on hours of voluntary practice and a performance score. The researcher tests whether the variables are associated. Select a suitable test and justify it.
back:
Model answer

Spearman’s rho is appropriate to test a relationship between two co-variables when scores are ordinal/ranked. It tests association, not causation.

Marking points

  • Relationship question, not difference
  • Two co-variables
  • Ordinal/ranked data linked to Spearman

Common trap

Do not infer causation from a correlation.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Psychology 7182 – Mark Scheme::Assessment skills::Statistics

front: A person repeatedly checks a locked door and reports intrusive fears that it is open. Classify examples and link them to OCD.
back:
Model answer

The intrusive fear is an obsession (cognitive); repeated checking is a compulsion (behavioural), often performed to reduce anxiety.

Marking points

  • Correct symptom categories and functional relation.

Common trap

Reversing obsession/compulsion or treating all worry as OCD.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Psychology 7182 – Mark Scheme::Clinical psychology and mental health

front: A patient has damage near the left frontal language region and struggles to produce fluent speech. Identify the likely area and explain.
back:
Model answer

Broca's area is associated with speech production; damage there may impair fluent speech. Language depends on interacting networks, so the area is not a stand-alone speech 'switch'.

Marking points

  • Identify correct area and function
  • cautious localisation.

Common trap

Confusing Broca's with Wernicke's area.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Psychology 7182 – Mark Scheme::Biopsychology

front: A researcher explains a child’s classroom aggression solely through inherited neural activity. Explain one strength and one limitation of this explanation.
back:
Model answer

It gives a specific biological mechanism that may generate testable predictions. It is reductionist because it leaves out interactions with learning, relationships and classroom context; those factors may alter when aggression occurs.

Marking points

  • Name biological reductionism and specify the biological level
  • Explain testability as a strength
  • Identify omitted contextual/psychological factors and why they matter

Common trap

Avoid treating “reductionist” as synonymous with false; judge what the explanation can and cannot account for.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Psychology 7182 – Mark Scheme::Issues and debates::Exam application

front: A memory study uses an unfamiliar word-list task in a quiet laboratory. Explain one validity issue and one improvement.
back:
Model answer

The artificial task may have limited ecological validity because recalling isolated words in a lab differs from everyday remembering. Use a realistic but controlled memory task, while keeping instructions and scoring standardised.

Marking points

  • Name a relevant validity type
  • Link study feature to the validity limitation
  • Give feasible improvement and trade-off/control

Common trap

Do not call the task realistic merely because it is controlled.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Psychology 7182 – Mark Scheme::Assessment skills::Validity

front: The same patients are classified as improved, unchanged or worsened after treatment. Explain why the sign test may fit and identify the sign-test value.
back:
Model answer

The sign test compares paired observations by direction of change. Exclude unchanged cases and count each direction: s is the less frequent sign count. The question gives no frequencies, so a numerical value cannot be calculated.

Marking points

  • Identify a difference between paired observations
  • Exclude ties and use the smaller sign count
  • Explain why a numerical value is unavailable

Common trap

Do not invent counts or include unchanged cases.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Psychology 7182 – Mark Scheme::Assessment skills::Statistics

front: Explain how a psychodynamic account differs from a humanistic account of personality.
back:
Model answer

Freud's psychodynamic account emphasises unconscious conflict among id, ego and superego and early psychosexual development. Humanistic psychology emphasises conscious experience, free will and the drive toward self-actualisation.

Marking points

  • Accurate contrast in mechanisms and view of agency.

Common trap

Attributing self-actualisation to Freud or unconscious drives to Rogers.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Psychology 7182 – Mark Scheme::Approaches in psychology

front: A study across eight student samples found delinquency associated with higher psychoticism and extraversion, but not neuroticism. How should this evidence be used to evaluate Eysenck’s criminal personality account?
back:
Model answer

The association with psychoticism and extraversion supports part of the predicted profile. The lack of a neuroticism association is inconsistent with the full prediction. Because personality and delinquency were measured rather than experimentally manipulated, the finding is correlational and does not establish that those traits cause offending.

Marking points

  • Link the observed P/E associations to partial support
  • Identify the absent N association as a challenge to the complete prediction
  • Qualify causal conclusions because the study is correlational

Common trap

Do not claim an association proves that personality causes offending.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Psychology 7182 – Mark Scheme::Forensic psychology::Biological explanations

front: Evaluate a restorative justice programme as a way of dealing with offending behaviour.
back:
Model answer

It can make the offender confront the consequences of the offence and may allow the victim to communicate the harm and discuss reparation. Its suitability depends on victim willingness, safety and offence context; a meeting is not appropriate in every case, so programme outcomes should not be assumed.

Marking points

  • Explain a plausible mechanism for accountability or victim voice
  • Develop a limitation grounded in suitability/safety/voluntariness
  • Make a qualified judgement

Common trap

Do not assume restorative justice is suitable or effective for every victim or offence.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Psychology 7182 – Mark Scheme::Forensic psychology::Exam evaluation

front: A question asks you to improve an investigation and explain why. What response structure turns a suggestion into an assessable point?
back:
Model answer

Name a specific change, apply it to the described procedure, then explain the methodological consequence (for example, define “on-task” as looking at the worksheet or writing, then train observers to use that code, improving inter-observer agreement).

Marking points

  • Specific change, not generic advice
  • Application to scenario detail
  • Explain effect on quality/data

Common trap

Do not name a change without explaining its effect on data quality.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Psychology 7182 – Mark Scheme::Assessment skills

front: Explain one strength and one limitation of the biological approach.
back:
Model answer

Biological explanations can be tested with objective measures such as brain imaging and can support useful interventions. However, correlations between biology and behaviour do not alone show direction of causation, and biological accounts may understate learning or social context.

Marking points

  • Specific strength + specific limitation + reasoning.

Common trap

Treating brain imaging as proof of causation.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Psychology 7182 – Mark Scheme::Approaches in psychology

front: Two independent groups choose one of three study locations. The researcher tests whether choice frequencies differ by group. Select a suitable test and justify it.
back:
Model answer

Chi-squared is appropriate because the outcome is nominal categories recorded as frequencies and the groups are independent; compare observed with expected frequencies.

Marking points

  • Test concerns frequency/category association or difference
  • Nominal data
  • Independent observations/groups

Common trap

Do not choose a correlation test for categorical frequency data.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Psychology 7182 – Mark Scheme::Assessment skills::Statistics

front: A worker refuses an unsafe instruction after a colleague also objects. Explain resistance using two concepts.
back:
Model answer

The colleague provides social support, so the worker is less isolated and authority pressure is weakened. If the worker has an internal locus of control, they may also feel personal responsibility for outcomes and act independently.

Marking points

  • Apply support and internal LoC separately
  • causal link to resistance.

Common trap

Presenting LoC as a fixed guarantee.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Psychology 7182 – Mark Scheme::Social influence

front: A question asks for one strength and one limitation of the working-memory model. Give an evidence-based response.
back:
Model answer

Dual-task research supports separate components: people can perform a verbal task alongside a spatial task more easily than two tasks competing for the same component. However, the central executive is underspecified, so the model is less precise about how attentional control works.

Marking points

  • Evidence tied to separate components
  • limitation tied to explanatory specificity.

Common trap

Listing generic 'too simplistic' without explaining what is missing.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Psychology 7182 – Mark Scheme::Memory

front: A unanimous group gives a clearly wrong answer. One peer quietly disagrees. Explain how this may affect conformity.
back:
Model answer

The dissenter breaks unanimity and provides social support. This can reduce normative pressure and give the participant confidence to answer independently; Asch found that a dissenting ally reduced conformity.

Marking points

  • Apply ally/dissent → reduced unanimity/NSI → resistance
  • connect to Asch evidence.

Common trap

Claiming a dissenter proves the participant privately changed their belief.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Psychology 7182 – Mark Scheme::Social influence

front: A client fears dogs. Outline systematic desensitisation and explain why it may reduce fear.
back:
Model answer

The therapist teaches relaxation, constructs a graded hierarchy from least to most feared dog-related situations, then pairs relaxation with gradual exposure up the hierarchy. Relaxation is incompatible with the conditioned fear response, supporting counterconditioning.

Marking points

  • Relaxation → hierarchy → gradual exposure → counterconditioning.

Common trap

Describing flooding (immediate high-intensity exposure) instead.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Psychology 7182 – Mark Scheme::Clinical psychology and mental health

front: A study of workplace leadership samples only men, then claims its findings explain all workers. Explain two issues relevant to gender and cultural bias.
back:
Model answer

The male-only sample risks androcentrism because male experience is treated as the norm; claiming all workers may lack universality. If the sample comes from one cultural setting, generalising across cultures may be ethnocentric unless contextual differences are considered.

Marking points

  • Identify male-centred sampling as androcentrism
  • Link the overgeneralised claim to limited universality
  • Explain cross-cultural generalisation as ethnocentric if one culture’s norms are assumed universal

Common trap

Do not say any gender difference automatically proves alpha bias; alpha concerns exaggerating differences.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Psychology 7182 – Mark Scheme::Issues and debates::Exam application

front: Explain how a falsifiable hypothesis and replication support psychological science.
back:
Model answer

A falsifiable hypothesis makes a prediction that evidence could contradict. Researchers test it empirically; a sufficiently clear method lets other researchers replicate the study and check whether the result is reliable, refining theory when evidence accumulates.

Marking points

  • Falsifiability means potentially disconfirmable prediction
  • Empirical test relates evidence to prediction
  • Replication enables independent checking/refinement

Common trap

Do not call a claim scientific if no possible result could contradict it.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Psychology 7182 – Mark Scheme::Assessment skills::Science

front: Evaluate Bandura, Ross and Ross’s Bobo-doll study as evidence for social learning theory.
back:
Model answer

The controlled comparison of children who observed aggressive, non-aggressive or no models supports the claim that observed behaviour can be imitated. However, the playroom and inflatable doll are artificial, short-term measures, so the study does not show that children will commit serious aggression in everyday life.

Marking points

  • Identify the relevant model-observation procedure and imitative-aggression finding.
  • Explain how the result supports observational learning.
  • Evaluate artificial setting or limits on generalising measured play to real-world aggression.

Common trap

Do not claim that the study proves media violence causes long-term criminal aggression.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Psychology 7182 – Mark Scheme::Approaches in psychology::Learning approaches

front: Explain how the brain can recover some function after trauma.
back:
Model answer

Plasticity allows undamaged regions to reorganise and support functions previously performed by damaged areas. Axonal sprouting or unmasking of existing pathways can help, although recovery is limited by injury extent and time.

Marking points

  • Plasticity → specific process → qualified outcome.

Common trap

Claiming every lost function fully returns.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Psychology 7182 – Mark Scheme::Biopsychology

front: Scores are 2, 4 and 6. Using the population standard-deviation procedure, calculate the standard deviation.
back:
Model answer

Mean = 4. Deviations are −2, 0, +2; squared deviations total 8. Population variance = 8/3, so SD = √(8/3) ≈ 1.63 (to 3 s.f.).

Marking points

  • Find mean and deviations
  • Square deviations and calculate mean squared deviation
  • Square root and round appropriately

Common trap

Do not divide by N−1 when the question specifies the population procedure.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Psychology 7182 – Mark Scheme::Assessment skills::Maths

front: A researcher tests whether instrumental music affects proofreading accuracy. Suggest a repeated-measures procedure and explain one control.
back:
Model answer

Each participant proofreads one text in silence and a matched text with instrumental music; counterbalance the order across participants to reduce practice or fatigue effects. Keep timing, text difficulty and instructions consistent, then compare the number of errors each participant correctly identifies.

Marking points

  • Specify same participants in both conditions
  • Operationalise the DV as errors correctly identified (or equivalent)
  • Use counterbalancing/standardisation and explain its purpose

Common trap

Do not leave all participants in the same condition order.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Psychology 7182 – Mark Scheme::Assessment skills::Design

front: Explain how learning theory and Bowlby's theory differ about why attachment forms.
back:
Model answer

Learning theory explains attachment through association with food and reinforcement of caregiver proximity. Bowlby proposed an innate attachment system and monotropy: an especially important primary attachment supports survival and later relationships.

Marking points

  • Describe both mechanisms
  • contrast learned secondary drive with evolved attachment.

Common trap

Saying Bowlby believed attachment was learned by feeding.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Psychology 7182 – Mark Scheme::Attachment

front: A police team infers a suspect’s likely home area from a series of offence locations, while another team classifies a crime scene as organised. Distinguish the approaches.
back:
Model answer

Inferring a likely home area from offence locations is geographical profiling, a data-driven method. Classifying the crime scene as organised uses the typology approach, which is typology-based and assigns a predefined category.

Marking points

  • Correctly identify geographical profiling from location pattern
  • Classify it as data-driven/bottom-up
  • Identify organised/disorganised profiling as typology/top-down

Common trap

Do not present a profile category as definitive identification of a suspect.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Psychology 7182 – Mark Scheme::Forensic psychology::Exam comparison

front: Compare Beck's and Ellis's cognitive explanations of depression.
back:
Model answer

Beck emphasises negative schemas and the triad of negative views of self, world and future. Ellis emphasises irrational beliefs about activating events, which produce emotional consequences. Both locate depression in maladaptive thinking and support CBT, but focus on different cognitive processes.

Marking points

  • Accurate components
  • shared cognitive premise
  • precise distinction.

Common trap

Calling A in Ellis's model the emotion (it is the activating event).
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Psychology 7182 – Mark Scheme::Clinical psychology and mental health

front: In an observation, 18 of 60 children share a toy at least once. Give the fraction and percentage who did so.
back:
Model answer

The fraction is 18/60 = 3/10. Percentage = (18 ÷ 60) × 100 = 30%.

Marking points

  • Calculate part/whole fraction
  • Simplify fraction correctly
  • Calculate percentage

Common trap

Do not use 18 as the denominator.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Psychology 7182 – Mark Scheme::Assessment skills::Maths

front: In a Paper 3 extended response, what makes the reasoning sustained and relevant?
back:
Model answer

Construct a coherent, logically ordered line of reasoning that answers the wording, develops claims, substantiates points with relevant psychology, and reaches a judgement where the command requires evaluation. Keep knowledge accurate and connect application to the stated context.

Marking points

  • Answer the question set and maintain a clear argument
  • Use relevant, accurate specification knowledge
  • Develop explanation/evaluation instead of listing points
  • Make scenario links explicit when asked to apply
  • Use a reasoned conclusion for an evaluative judgement

Common trap

A generic topic summary can contain accurate knowledge yet fail to address the question or apply it to the given context.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Psychology 7182 – Mark Scheme::Paper 3 assessment::Extended responses

front: This practice scattergram uses invented data for eight volunteers. What does it suggest about hours of sleep and puzzle completion time? Explain one reason a causal conclusion is unwarranted.
back:
Model answer

There is a strong negative association. Volunteers who reported more sleep generally took less time. Puzzle familiarity could be related to both sleep habits and completion time, so the association alone cannot establish that sleep caused faster performance.

Marking points

  • State the direction using both co-variables.
  • Describe the overall pattern and allow for the exception.
  • Give a plausible third variable and explain why it limits a causal claim.

Common trap

A lower completion time means faster performance; a negative association can therefore indicate better performance.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Psychology 7182 – Mark Scheme::Research methods::Data presentation

front: Evaluate CBT as a treatment for depression.
back:
Model answer

CBT teaches patients to identify and challenge unhelpful thoughts, matching cognitive explanations and giving them skills they can use after treatment. It can be effective, but access, engagement and severity matter; some patients may benefit from medication or combined care.

Marking points

  • Mechanism → appropriateness/effectiveness → qualified limitation.

Common trap

Claiming CBT works for everyone or giving unsupported cure rates.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Psychology 7182 – Mark Scheme::Clinical psychology and mental health

front: A study finds that students reporting more hours of sleep also tend to report higher concentration ratings. State what can and cannot be concluded.
back:
Model answer

The variables show a positive correlation: higher reported sleep is associated with higher concentration ratings. The result does not show that sleep caused concentration to improve; concentration could affect sleep reports, or a third variable such as workload could influence both.

Marking points

  • State direction accurately
  • Describe association between co-variables
  • Avoid causal claim and give plausible alternative explanation

Common trap

Do not infer causation from a positive correlation.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Psychology 7182 – Mark Scheme::Assessment skills::Correlation

front: A group’s scores are 2, 4, 4, 6 and 9. Give the mean, median, mode and range.
back:
Model answer

Mean = (2+4+4+6+9) ÷ 5 = 5; median = 4; mode = 4; range = 9−2 = 7.

Marking points

  • Correct total and division for mean
  • Correct ordered middle score and mode
  • Correct range subtraction

Common trap

Do not use the largest score as the range.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Psychology 7182 – Mark Scheme::Assessment skills::Statistics

front: A teacher models the first steps of a puzzle, gives prompts when needed, then gradually withdraws help. Explain this using Vygotsky.
back:
Model answer

The puzzle may lie within the learner’s ZPD if they cannot yet solve it alone but can succeed with help. The teacher’s prompts are scaffolding; withdrawing them as competence grows supports independent performance.

Marking points

  • Define the learner’s assisted-versus-independent range as ZPD
  • Identify prompts/modeling as scaffolding
  • Link fading support to growing independence

Common trap

Do not describe the zone of proximal development as a task already mastered alone.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Psychology 7182 – Mark Scheme::Cognition and development::Exam application

front: A researcher records every time children interrupt during a 20-minute play session. Propose one way to improve the observation’s reliability.
back:
Model answer

Define “interrupt” with observable inclusion/exclusion rules, train observers to apply the categories, and have two observers independently code a sample so agreement can be checked.

Marking points

  • Operationalise behavioural category
  • Use independent observers or training
  • Explain reliability as consistency/agreement

Common trap

Do not mistake accuracy of a single observer for agreement between observers.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Psychology 7182 – Mark Scheme::Assessment skills::Observation

front: Give one advantage and one limitation of fMRI for investigating brain function.
back:
Model answer

fMRI provides a non-invasive image with good spatial resolution and can show which regions are more active during a task. Its signal is an indirect, relatively slow blood-oxygenation measure, so it cannot establish that activation caused the behaviour.

Marking points

  • Advantage tied to spatial localisation
  • limitation tied to indirect BOLD/time/cause.

Common trap

Saying fMRI directly measures electrical firing.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Psychology 7182 – Mark Scheme::Biopsychology

front: Students plan to investigate whether exam-related imagery changes mood using a short questionnaire. State one risk and a control before data collection.
back:
Model answer

Questions could cause distress or disclose sensitive information. Avoid intrusive wording, make participation voluntary, allow skipping/stopping, protect responses, and have a clear support/referral and stop procedure approved before data collection.

Marking points

  • Identify plausible psychological/privacy risk
  • Give proportionate prevention/control
  • Include stop/support procedure

Common trap

Do not collect identifiable responses without explaining how privacy is protected.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Psychology 7182 – Mark Scheme::Assessment skills::Practical skills

front: Evaluate using animal research to explain human attachment.
back:
Model answer

Lorenz and Harlow offer controlled evidence that early experience and contact comfort can shape attachment-like behaviour. However, findings in geese or rhesus monkeys cannot be transferred directly to human attachment, which is influenced by complex social and cultural factors.

Marking points

  • Specific evidence → value of control/comparative insight → species/generalisation limitation.

Common trap

Treating animal findings as direct proof of Bowlby's human theory.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Psychology 7182 – Mark Scheme::Attachment

front: A researcher interviews participants about their experiences and then counts how many mention each theme. Classify the original and coded data.
back:
Model answer

The interview accounts are qualitative primary data; once responses are coded into theme frequencies, those counts are quantitative data derived from the primary material.

Marking points

  • Identify qualitative interview accounts
  • Identify coding process
  • Classify resulting counts as quantitative

Common trap

Do not assume counts remain qualitative just because they came from interviews.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Psychology 7182 – Mark Scheme::Assessment skills::Data

front: After assaulting someone, a person says, “They were asking for it, and no one was really hurt.” Apply two cognitive explanations.
back:
Model answer

The second statement downplays harm and illustrates minimalisation. The first blames the victim, but does not establish hostile attribution bias: we would need evidence that the person interpreted an ambiguous action as hostile. Victim blaming alone is insufficient to establish that interpretation.

Marking points

  • Apply minimalisation to downplaying harm
  • Explain that hostile attribution requires perceived hostility
  • Recognise that the scenario does not establish it

Common trap

Do not treat all victim blaming as evidence of hostile attribution bias.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Psychology 7182 – Mark Scheme::Forensic psychology::Exam application

front: The same participants rank stress before and after a relaxation exercise. The researcher predicts a change. Select a suitable test and justify it.
back:
Model answer

Wilcoxon signed-ranks is appropriate: this is a test of difference between related observations, with ordinal ranked scores.

Marking points

  • Difference rather than relationship
  • Related/repeated design
  • Ordinal/non-parametric data linked to Wilcoxon

Common trap

Do not choose an unrelated test for the same participants.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Psychology 7182 – Mark Scheme::Assessment skills::Statistics

front: A witness hears another witness describe a red coat before giving their own account. Explain a risk to accuracy.
back:
Model answer

This is post-event discussion: the other person's account can become incorporated into or confused with the witness's memory, creating memory conformity.

Marking points

  • Identify PED → mechanism of contamination/conformity → possible inaccurate report.

Common trap

Saying the original memory is necessarily erased.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Psychology 7182 – Mark Scheme::Memory

front: Explain how the two-process model accounts for both acquisition and maintenance of a phobia.
back:
Model answer

A neutral stimulus may be paired with an aversive event through classical conditioning, producing fear. Avoiding the stimulus reduces anxiety, so negative reinforcement maintains avoidance and prevents corrective learning.

Marking points

  • Separate acquisition from maintenance
  • specify conditioning mechanism at each stage.

Common trap

Describing avoidance as positive reinforcement.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Psychology 7182 – Mark Scheme::Clinical psychology and mental health

front: Explain why a person may conform in an ambiguous situation but privately accept the group's answer.
back:
Model answer

When the answer is unclear, the person may use the group as information (ISI). If they believe the group is right, they internalise its view, changing both public behaviour and private belief.

Marking points

  • Identify ISI → ambiguity/informational reliance → private acceptance/internalisation.

Common trap

Calling every conformity response compliance.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Psychology 7182 – Mark Scheme::Social influence

front: Contrast the behaviourist and cognitive approaches to studying memory.
back:
Model answer

Behaviourists explain behaviour through observable stimulus-response learning and consequences. Cognitive psychologists infer internal processes, such as memory structures, from performance and use models to explain them.

Marking points

  • Contrast observable learning vs inferred mental processes
  • do not caricature cognitive work as direct observation of thoughts.

Common trap

Saying cognitive psychologists can directly observe memory.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Psychology 7182 – Mark Scheme::Approaches in psychology

front: Compare the agentic-state explanation with the authoritarian-personality explanation of obedience.
back:
Model answer

The agentic-state account explains obedience through a situational shift of responsibility to a legitimate authority. The authoritarian-personality account attributes obedience to a relatively enduring disposition. Thus one emphasises context and the other individual differences.

Marking points

  • Define both accurately
  • compare locus of cause
  • optionally apply to a scenario.

Common trap

Treating the two explanations as mutually exclusive or using 'agentic' to mean blind obedience.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Psychology 7182 – Mark Scheme::Social influence

front:
The table shows made-up scores for the same students before and after a study-skills workshop. Calculate the sign test statistic s and state the effective N.
StudentBeforeAfter
156
247
377
485
535
664
769
856
977
1048
back:
Model answer

Assign each pair the sign of after minus before. Ignore the two ties. There are six + signs and two − signs, so the less frequent count is s = 2 and the effective N = 8.
StudentBeforeAfterChange
156+
247+
3770
485−
535+
664−
769+
856+

1048+

Marking points

  • Exclude ties from counts
  • Count remaining + and − correctly
  • Set s to less frequent sign and give effective N

Common trap

Do not count zero differences as either sign or include them in the effective N.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Psychology 7182 – Mark Scheme::Assessment skills::Statistics

front: A clinician is considering a diagnosis after a patient reports hearing voices and has persistent low motivation. Identify one symptom of each type and one diagnostic caution.
back:
Model answer

Hearing voices is a positive symptom (a hallucination); persistent low motivation is consistent with avolition, a negative symptom. Diagnosis should consider symptom overlap and comorbidity and avoid assuming one report alone is sufficient.

Marking points

  • Classify hallucination as positive
  • Classify avolition as negative
  • Name and apply a diagnostic caution

Common trap

Do not label low motivation a delusion; avolition is a negative symptom.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Psychology 7182 – Mark Scheme::Schizophrenia::Exam application

front: A child says there is more juice after the same amount is poured into a taller, narrower glass. Use Piaget’s theory to explain the response.
back:
Model answer

The child is showing difficulty with conservation, characteristic of pre-operational thinking. The taller appearance dominates the child’s judgement, indicating the child has not yet coordinated the relevant dimensions of the situation.

Marking points

  • Identify conservation as the relevant concept
  • Apply the child’s judgement to pre-operational thinking
  • Explain the appearance-based reasoning

Common trap

Do not explain the answer with object permanence; it concerns continued existence of hidden objects.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Psychology 7182 – Mark Scheme::Cognition and development::Exam application

front: In an Issues and Debates response, how should you use a topic example?
back:
Model answer

Name the relevant debate, identify a specific theory, finding or method from a studied topic, then explain exactly how it illustrates the debate. For example, a biological account can illustrate determinism only if you explain how it treats behaviour as caused by biological factors.

Marking points

  • Identify the debate accurately
  • Use relevant specification-topic knowledge
  • Make the link explicit rather than merely listing an example

Common trap

A topic name without an explained link does not demonstrate how it illustrates the debate.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Psychology 7182 – Mark Scheme::Issues and debates::Integration

front: A witness sees an event in the rain, then is interviewed in a dry room. Suggest a cognitive-interview technique and explain its use.
back:
Model answer

The interviewer could ask the witness to mentally reinstate the rain, sounds and feelings present at the event. Context reinstatement may restore matching cues and improve access to the event memory.

Marking points

  • Name technique → concrete context detail → retrieval-cue rationale.

Common trap

Treating reinstatement as hypnosis or assuming it guarantees accuracy.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Psychology 7182 – Mark Scheme::Memory

front: A researcher has completed a study but another researcher cannot reproduce the procedure from the report. Which section needs improvement and what should be included?
back:
Model answer

The method section needs enough detail to reproduce the design, participants, materials/measures and procedure, including operational definitions and relevant controls.

Marking points

  • Name method section
  • Give reproducibility detail
  • Link clarity to replication

Common trap

Do not put the procedural detail only in the discussion section.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Psychology 7182 – Mark Scheme::Assessment skills::Reporting

front: Explain why recall of a word list may be poor after learning two similar lists.
back:
Model answer

The lists compete for retrieval because they share features. If the first list disrupts recall of the second, this is proactive interference; if the second disrupts recall of the first, it is retroactive interference.

Marking points

  • Identify similarity/competition
  • correctly map direction to target.

Common trap

Reversing proactive and retroactive.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Psychology 7182 – Mark Scheme::Memory

front: A child watches a model praised for sharing, then shares a toy. Explain this using social learning theory.
back:
Model answer

The child attends to and remembers the model's behaviour; seeing praise is vicarious reinforcement, increasing motivation to imitate. The child must also be able to reproduce the action.

Marking points

  • Model → mediational process(es) → vicarious reinforcement → imitation.

Common trap

Calling the observed praise direct reinforcement of the child.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Psychology 7182 – Mark Scheme::Approaches in psychology

front: Evaluate using antipsychotic medication as the only treatment for schizophrenia.
back:
Model answer

Medication can reduce symptoms for some people, making it a useful component of care. As a sole approach it may not address cognitive difficulties, family stress or social needs, and adverse effects can affect adherence; an interactionist plan can combine approaches according to need.

Marking points

  • Explain a plausible benefit of drug therapy
  • Develop a limitation tied to side effects or unaddressed needs
  • Reach a reasoned judgement favouring individualised combined care

Common trap

Avoid claiming medication cures schizophrenia or works equally for everyone.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Psychology 7182 – Mark Scheme::Schizophrenia::Exam evaluation

front: Trace a neural impulse from receptor toward a muscle response.
back:
Model answer

In one possible pathway, a sensory neuron carries input to the CNS; a relay neuron passes it within the CNS; a motor neuron carries output to a muscle. At synapses, neurotransmitters cross the cleft and may excite or inhibit the next neuron.

Marking points

  • Correct pathway and synaptic transmission
  • distinguish neuron classes.

Common trap

Placing the relay neuron outside CNS or saying neurotransmitters travel along axons between neurons.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Psychology 7182 – Mark Scheme::Biopsychology

front: A one-tailed test has an observed value beyond the .05 critical value in the predicted direction. State the decision and one conclusion limit.
back:
Model answer

The result is significant at p ≤ .05, so reject the null hypothesis in favour of evidence consistent with the directional alternative. Significance does not show the effect is large, important or causal.

Marking points

  • Compare observed and critical values using test convention
  • State p level and null decision
  • Avoid equating significance with size/importance

Common trap

Do not treat statistical significance as proof of a large or causal effect.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Psychology 7182 – Mark Scheme::Assessment skills::Statistics

front: A child explores while checking back with a caregiver, becomes upset at separation, and is readily comforted at reunion. Identify the pattern and justify it.
back:
Model answer

Secure attachment: the caregiver acts as a secure base for exploration, separation causes distress, and reunion restores comfort.

Marking points

  • Correct pattern + two or more matching behaviours.

Common trap

Using a single behaviour as a definitive diagnosis outside the Strange Situation context.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Psychology 7182 – Mark Scheme::Attachment

front: A student claims the ERA study proves that institutional deprivation causes permanent damage. Improve the claim.
back:
Model answer

ERA findings linked severe early deprivation with later difficulties, especially after longer deprivation, but many children showed recovery after adoption. Because children were not randomly assigned to deprivation or adoption timing, the study supports an association and timing-related pattern rather than proving inevitable permanent damage.

Marking points

  • Accurate result pattern → recovery nuance → design/cause limitation.

Common trap

Treating six months as a deterministic cut-off or 'Romanian' as cause itself.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Psychology 7182 – Mark Scheme::Attachment

front: A frequency table records 3, 5 and 2 participants choosing options A, B and C. State the modal category and the percentage choosing B.
back:
Model answer

B is modal with a frequency of 5. Total frequency is 10, so B = (5 ÷ 10) × 100 = 50%.

Marking points

  • Identify category with greatest frequency
  • Find total frequency
  • Calculate percentage correctly

Common trap

Do not divide the frequency for B by the number of categories.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Psychology 7182 – Mark Scheme::Assessment skills::Displays

front: A teacher wants to compare students’ anxiety scores before and after a timed memory task. Participants are told the task is about memory only; some feel embarrassed by low scores. Identify an ethical issue and give a workable response.
back:
Model answer

The incomplete explanation risks undermining informed consent, and the task may cause embarrassment. Explain the task’s relevant demands and right to stop before consent; minimise evaluative framing, protect scores, debrief participants and offer withdrawal of identifiable data.

Marking points

  • Identify the ethical concern
  • Give a concrete safeguard matched to it
  • Explain how the safeguard reduces risk

Common trap

“Get consent” alone is not enough: state what participants need to know and how the procedure protects them.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Psychology 7182 – Mark Scheme::Assessment skills::Ethics
